== Problem ==
Let <math>(a,b,c,d)</math> be an ordered quadruple of not necessarily distinct integers, each one of them in the set <math>\{0,1,2,3\}.</math> For how many such quadruples is it true that <math>a\cdot d-b\cdot c</math> is odd? (For example, <math>(0,3,1,1)</math> is one such quadruple, because <math>0\cdot 1-3\cdot 1 = -3</math> is odd.)

<math>\textbf{(A) } 48 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 64 \qquad \textbf{(C) } 96 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 128 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 192</math>

==Solutions==
===Solution 1 (Parity)===
In order for <imath>a\cdot d-b\cdot c</imath> to be odd, consider parity. We must have (even)-(odd) or (odd)-(even). There are <imath>2(2 + 4) = 12</imath> ways to pick numbers to obtain an even product. There are <imath>2 \cdot 2 = 4</imath> ways to obtain an odd product. Therefore, the total amount of ways to make <imath>a\cdot d-b\cdot c</imath> odd is <imath>2 \cdot (12 \cdot 4) = \boxed{\bold{(C)}\ 96}</imath>.

~Midnight

===Solution 2 (Solution 1 but more in-depth)===

Consider parity. We need exactly one term to be odd, one term to be even. Because of symmetry, we can set <imath>ad</imath> to be odd and <imath>bc</imath> to be even, then multiply by <imath>2.</imath> If <imath>ad</imath> is odd, both <imath>a</imath> and <imath>d</imath> must be odd, therefore there are <imath>2\cdot2=4</imath> possibilities for <imath>ad.</imath> Consider <imath>bc.</imath> Let us say that <imath>b</imath> is even. Then there are <imath>2\cdot4=8</imath> possibilities for <imath>bc.</imath> However, <imath>b</imath> can be odd, in which case we have <imath>2\cdot2=4</imath> more possibilities for <imath>bc.</imath> Thus there are <imath>12</imath> ways for us to choose <imath>bc</imath> and <imath>4</imath> ways for us to choose <imath>ad.</imath> Therefore, also considering symmetry, we have <imath>2 \cdot 4 \cdot 12= \boxed{ \text{(C) } 96}</imath> total values of <imath>ad-bc.</imath>

~lpieleanu (Reformatting and Minor Edits)

===Solution 3 (Complementary Counting)===
There are 4 ways to choose any number independently and 2 ways to choose any odd number independently.
To get an even products, we count: <imath>\text{P(any number)} \cdot \text{P(any number)}-\text{P(odd)}\cdot\text{P(odd)}</imath>, which is <imath>4 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot 2=12</imath>.
The number of ways to get an odd product can be counted like so: <imath>\text{P(odd)}\cdot\text{P(odd)}</imath>, which is <imath>2 \cdot 2</imath>, or <imath>4</imath>.
So, for one product to be odd the other to be even: <imath>2 \cdot 4 \cdot 12= \boxed{ \text{(C) } 96}</imath> (order matters). 

~Anonymous and Arctic_Bunny

===Solution 4 (Solution 3 but more in-depth)===
We use complementary counting: If the difference is even, then we can subtract those cases. There are a total of <imath>4^4=256</imath> cases.

For an even difference, we have (even)-(even) or (odd-odd). 

From Solution 3:

"There are 4 ways to choose any number independently and 2 ways to choose any odd number independently.
even products:(number)*(number)-(odd)*(odd): <imath>4 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot 2=12</imath>.
odd products: (odd)*(odd): <imath>2 \cdot 2 =4</imath>."

With this, we easily calculate <imath>256-12^2-4^2=\textbf{(C)96}</imath>.

~kevinmathz

===Solution 5 (Casework)===
As in solution 1, we must have (even)-(odd) or (odd)-(even). We see that there are two cases, if <imath>ad</imath> is even and <imath>bc</imath> is odd and if <imath>ad</imath> is odd and <imath>bc</imath> is even. Because of symmetry, we can multiply by two for when <imath>ad</imath> is odd and <imath>bc</imath> is even. Let <imath>e</imath> denote an even number and let <imath>o</imath> denote an odd number. 

If <imath>ad</imath> is even and <imath>bc</imath> is odd, there are three cases:


<cmath>(e,o,o,e)</cmath>
<cmath>(e,o,o,o)</cmath>
<cmath>(o,o,o,e)</cmath>


For each of these cases, there are <imath>2^4</imath> ways to choose from the set <imath>(0,1,2,3)</imath> as there are 2 even's and 2 odd's; because there are three cases, we multiply this by 3. Also, because of there are 2 cases (<imath>ad</imath> is even and <imath>bc</imath> is odd and if <imath>ad</imath> is odd and <imath>bc</imath> is even), we multiply this by 2. This gives us:

<imath>2^4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2= \textbf{(C)96}</imath>

===Solution 6===
For parity reasons, if <imath>ad - bc</imath> is to be odd, we must have <imath>ad</imath> odd and <imath>bc</imath> even or <imath>ad</imath> even and <imath>bc</imath> odd. By symmetry, these cases are identical, so we consider the first one and multiply by two at the end. For <imath>ad</imath> to be odd, we must have both <imath>a</imath> and <imath>d</imath> odd, and there are <imath>2 \cdot 2</imath> ways to do so. To count the cases where <imath>bc</imath> is odd, we use PIE. there are <imath>2 \cdot 4 = 8</imath> ways for <imath>b</imath> to be odd and <imath>4 \cdot 2 = 8</imath> ways for <imath>c</imath> to be odd, and there are <imath>2 \cdot 2 = 4</imath> ways for both to be odd. Thus, there are <imath>8 + 8 - 4 = 12</imath> ways for <imath>bc</imath> to be even. Multiplying out, there are <imath>2 \cdot 4 \cdot 12</imath> ways to have <imath>ad - bc</imath> odd for a total of <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C)}~96}</imath>.

~ [https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/User:Cxsmi cxsmi]

===Solution 7(Probability)===
Consider the scenario where each number in the quadruple is randomly picked uniformly from the set <imath>\{0,1,2,3\}</imath>. In that case the probability for <imath>ad</imath> and <imath>bc</imath> to be odd is <imath>\frac{1}{4}</imath>. Hence, the probability that <imath>ad-bc</imath> is odd is 

<imath>\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{3}{4} + \frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{8}</imath>

Clearly, there are <imath>4^4</imath> total outcomes from the uniform sample space, and thus the amount of ways is <imath>4^4 \cdot \frac{3}{8} = \boxed{\textbf{(C)}~96}</imath>.

~Arden

==Additional Notes==
===Additional Note 1===
When calculating the number of even products and odd products, since the only way to get an odd product is to multiply two odd integers together, and there are <math>2</math> odd integers, it can quickly be deduced that there are <math>2 \cdot 2 = 4</math> possibilities for an odd product. Since the product must be either odd or even, and there are <math>4 \cdot 4 = 16</math> ways to choose factors for the product, there are <math>16 - 4 = 12</math> possibilities for an even product. ~[[User:emerald_block|emerald_block]]
